title: Reception, Admission, Referral and Discharge Procedures
path: Reception, Admission, Referral and Discharge Procedures

headings.title: Introduction to Ward Reception and Orientation
headings.content: Ward reception and orientation mark the critical first impression a patient has of the healthcare facility and the nursing team. When a patient arrives at the ward, the receiving nurse must exhibit a warm, professional, and empathetic demeanor to alleviate the anxiety and fear commonly associated with hospitalization. The primary goal of reception is to establish therapeutic rapport and ensure the patient feels safe and valued. Immediate assessment must begin to identify any urgent physical or psychological needs, ensuring stabilization if the patient is acutely ill. Following the initial welcome, a comprehensive orientation to the ward environment is conducted. This process involves introducing the patient to the physical layout of the unit, including their bed space, the call bell system, bathroom facilities, and the dayroom. The nurse must also explain ward routines, such as meal times, visiting hours, doctor's rounds, and policies regarding personal belongings and safety precautions. In the Nigerian context, communicating clearly in a language the patient or their accompanying relatives understand—whether English, Pidgin, or local languages—is vital for reducing apprehension and promoting compliance. Orientation empowers the patient, fostering a sense of control and partnership in their care plan from day one.

headings.title: Types and Procedures of Hospital Admission
headings.content: Hospital admission is the formal process of accepting a patient into a healthcare facility for medical or surgical care, observation, or diagnostic evaluation. Admissions are broadly categorized into two main types: emergency admissions and elective or routine admissions. Emergency admissions occur suddenly and unexpectedly, often through the Accident and Emergency unit, due to acute trauma, severe illness, or life-threatening conditions requiring immediate medical intervention. In these cases, lifesaving procedures take precedence over rigorous administrative paperwork, which is usually completed by relatives later. Conversely, elective admissions are planned well in advance for scheduled surgeries, chronic disease investigations, or specialized treatments. The patient arrives with a referral letter or booking slip, having undergone pre-admission testing. The admission procedure requires meticulous nursing coordination. The nurse must prepare the bed space and necessary equipment prior to arrival, greet the patient warmly, perform baseline vital signs, conduct a systematic physical assessment, and reconcile any home medications. Additionally, safety measures such as fall risk assessments and identification bands must be applied immediately. Adhering to these structured procedures guarantees patient safety, legal compliance, and a seamless transition from the community or emergency setting into the inpatient ward environment.

headings.title: Documentation and Record Keeping During Admission
headings.content: Accurate documentation and meticulous record keeping during admission are fundamental legal and professional responsibilities of the nurse. The admission record serves as a legal document, a communication tool among members of the multidisciplinary healthcare team, and a baseline for evaluating ongoing patient care. Upon admission, the nurse opens the patient's case notes and inputs vital data, including demographic information, next of kin contacts, date and time of arrival, mode of arrival, and the presenting complaint. The admission nursing assessment form must be completed systematically, documenting baseline vital signs, height, weight, allergies, current medications, and physical findings. The nurse must also document a comprehensive nursing care plan based on identified problems and nursing diagnoses. In Nigerian healthcare facilities, whether using paper-based charts or electronic health records, documentation must be legible, factual, objective, and signed with the nurse's full signature and designation. Avoid vague terminology; instead, record exact quotes from the patient and precise measurements. Timely documentation prevents gaps in information, ensures continuity of care across different shifts, and provides legal protection for both the nurse and the healthcare institution in the event of any medico-legal disputes.

headings.title: Patient Referral: Principles, Types, and Procedures
headings.content: Patient referral is the process of directing or transferring a patient to a higher level of care, specialized facility, or specific healthcare professional when the current facility lacks the resources, expertise, or diagnostic tools to manage the patient's condition adequately. Referrals are guided by established principles of continuity of care, timeliness, and patient consent. There are various types of referrals, including internal referrals (from one department to another within the same hospital, such as from the medical ward to physiotherapy) and external referrals (from primary health centers to secondary general hospitals, or from secondary to tertiary teaching hospitals). The referral procedure requires meticulous planning and communication. The referring nurse must ensure the patient is as stable as possible before transit. A formal referral letter must be written, containing a concise clinical summary, results of investigations done, treatment given so far, and the specific reason for referral. Copies of relevant diagnostic reports, such as laboratory results and X-rays, must accompany the patient. Furthermore, the receiving facility must be contacted in advance to ensure bed availability and readiness. Effective referral mechanisms reduce maternal and child mortality, prevent delays in emergency treatment, and ensure patients receive specialized care appropriate for their health needs.

headings.title: Inter-Facility and Intra-Facility Transfer Guidelines
headings.content: Transfers involve moving a patient from one clinical area to another. They are classified into intra-facility transfers (moving within the same hospital, such as from the intensive care unit to the step-down ward) and inter-facility transfers (moving between two entirely separate hospitals). Both types require rigorous guidelines to ensure patient safety and prevent clinical deterioration during transit. Prior to any transfer, the nurse must obtain a medical order, inform the patient and their relatives, and secure the consent of the receiving unit or facility. A comprehensive handover must be prepared, highlighting the patient's current diagnosis, clinical status, ongoing treatments, intravenous lines, drainage tubes, and any specialized equipment required during transit. For critically ill patients, appropriate escort personnel must accompany the transfer, such as a medical doctor or a critical care nurse, along with emergency equipment like portable oxygen, suction machines, and crash carts. Documenting the exact time of transfer, mode of transport, and the condition of the patient upon arrival at the new location is mandatory. Adhering to these guidelines minimizes risks, ensures uninterrupted monitoring, and promotes optimal patient outcomes across different healthcare settings.

headings.title: Discharge Planning and Preparation
headings.content: Discharge planning is a multi-disciplinary, continuous process designed to ensure that a patient has a smooth and safe transition from the hospital setting to home or to another care facility. Effective discharge planning begins ideally at the point of admission and involves the patient, their family, nurses, doctors, pharmacists, and medical social workers. The goal is to identify the patient's post-discharge needs early, preventing unnecessary hospital readmissions and promoting optimal recovery. The nurse plays a central coordinating role in this process. Assessment of the home environment, family support systems, financial capabilities, and physical limitations is conducted. Based on these findings, the nurse coordinates education on medication administration, wound care, dietary modifications, activity restrictions, and signs of complications to report. In Nigeria, where family caregivers play a massive role in post-hospital care, educating the primary caregiver thoroughly is crucial. Follow-up appointments and necessary medical equipment, such as crutches or glucometers, are arranged prior to departure. Good discharge planning bridges the gap between hospital and home, empowering patients and families to manage health conditions confidently and safely.

headings.title: Types of Discharge and Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content: Discharge from a healthcare facility can occur under various circumstances, each carrying distinct nursing responsibilities. The primary types of discharge include routine (or regular) discharge, discharge against medical advice (DAMA), transfer discharge, and discharge by absconding. A routine discharge happens when a medical doctor certifies that the patient has recovered sufficiently and can continue recovery at home. Nursing responsibilities include returning personal valuables, providing written and verbal health education, handing over discharge medications and prescriptions, issuing appointment cards, and escorting the patient out. Conversely, discharge against medical advice (DAMA) occurs when a competent patient chooses to leave the hospital prematurely against the doctor's recommendations. In such cases, the nurse must inform the doctor immediately, educate the patient on the potential risks of leaving, document the event meticulously, and have the patient or legal guardian sign a DAMA form to protect the hospital legally. If a patient absconds (leaves secretly without notifying staff), the nurse must inform hospital management and security immediately and document the time and circumstances. Understanding these discharge types ensures legal protection, maintains accurate institutional records, and upholds professional nursing standards.
